**Key idea:** Register the signal once (`prev`) and AND the delayed copy with the inverted current value: `fall = prev & ~sig`. That pulse is high for exactly one clock after a 1→0 transition. In hardware it is one flip-flop, one inverter and one AND gate, plus an optional output flop to make the pulse glitch-free.

```wavedrom

  { "name": "clk",          "wave": "p........" },
  { "name": "sig (synced)", "wave": "01...0..." },
  { "name": "prev",         "wave": "0.1...0.." },
  { "name": "fall = prev & ~sig", "wave": "0....10.." },
  { "name": "fall_q (registered)", "wave": "0.....10." }
],
  "head": { "text": "fall is high for one cycle while prev=1 and sig=0" } }
```

### Synthesized circuit
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SIG["sig"] --> FF1["DFF prev"]
  CLK["clk"] --> FF1
  SIG --> INV["NOT"]
  FF1 -->|prev| AND["AND2"]
  INV -->|"~sig"| AND
  AND -->|fall comb| FF2["DFF (optional)"]
  CLK --> FF2
  FF2 --> OUT["fall_q"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module fall_edge_det (
  input  logic clk,
  input  logic rst_n,
  input  logic sig_async,   // may come from another clock domain
  output logic fall,        // combinational, same cycle as sampled edge
  output logic fall_q       // registered, glitch-free, 1 cycle later
);
  logic s1, s2, prev;

  // 2-flop synchronizer first if the source is asynchronous
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) {s2, s1} <= 2'b00;
    else        {s2, s1} <= {s1, sig_async};

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) prev <= 1'b0;   // reset value chosen so no false edge after reset
    else        prev <= s2;

  assign fall = prev & ~s2;

  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) fall_q <= 1'b0;
    else        fall_q <= fall;
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- Rising edge is the mirror: `rise = ~prev & sig`; any edge: `prev ^ sig`.
- Detecting on the synchronized signal (`s2`) is essential: feeding a raw async input straight into the AND gate can create a runt pulse or a pulse seen by only some loads.
- The registered version adds one cycle latency but gives a clean flop output for downstream logic or another domain.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Reset value of `prev`: if the line idles high, reset `prev` to 0 → no edge; if reset to 1 while `sig`=0 you get a spurious pulse right after reset.
- Pulses shorter than one destination clock period are lost; use a toggle/handshake synchronizer instead.
- Do not use `always @(negedge sig)` as a "detector" — that turns the data signal into a clock.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you detect both edges?* `edge = prev ^ sig`.
- *What if the input pulse is narrower than clk?* Capture it in the source domain (toggle flop) and synchronize the toggle.

**Key idea:** Grab a `process` handle inside each forked branch with `process::self()`, then call `kill()` on only the handle you want. `disable fork` kills every child of the calling process, and `disable <block_name>` kills every active activation of that named block, so neither one can stop a single branch reliably.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant P as parent
  participant A as branch A
  participant B as branch B
  participant C as branch C
  P->>A: fork (h[0] = process::self)
  P->>B: fork (h[1] = process::self)
  P->>C: fork (h[2] = process::self)
  P->>P: wait (h[1] != null)
  P->>B: h[1].kill()
  A-->>P: keeps running
  C-->>P: keeps running
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module tb;
  process h[3];

  task automatic worker(int id, int dly);
    h[id] = process::self();          // publish my handle
    repeat (5) begin
      #dly $display("%0t: worker %0d tick", $time, id);
    end
  endtask

  initial begin
    fork
      worker(0, 10);
      worker(1, 7);
      worker(2, 12);
    join_none

    // handles are assigned only after children start running
    wait (h[1] != null);
    #20;
    if (h[1].status() inside {process::RUNNING, process::WAITING,
                              process::SUSPENDED})
      h[1].kill();                    // only branch 1 stops
    wait fork;                        // 0 and 2 finish normally
    $display("%0t: done", $time);
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
| Mechanism | What it stops |
| --- | --- |
| `disable fork` | all descendants of the *current* process (including forks spawned earlier, e.g. by other components) |
| `disable blk_name` | every active instance of that named block, in any process |
| `h.kill()` | exactly that process and its descendants |

- `process::self()` is valid only inside the branch, so publish it into an array/queue as the first statement.
- `status()` returns `FINISHED`, `RUNNING`, `WAITING`, `SUSPENDED`, or `KILLED`. Check it before calling `kill()`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- With `join_none`, children have not started yet when the parent continues, so `h[1]` is still `null`. Wait for it, or `#0`.
- `kill()` does not release semaphores or mailboxes the branch was holding. Clean up yourself.
- A named block inside a task called from several places shares one name. `disable` hits all of them.

### Follow-ups
- *Kill all but one?* Loop over handles and skip the one to keep.
- *Pause instead of kill?* `h.suspend()` / `h.resume()`.

**Key idea:** Race the real work against a delay inside `fork ... join_any`. Whichever finishes first unblocks the parent. Then kill the loser with `disable fork`, but only after wrapping the whole thing in its own `fork begin ... end join` so the disable reaches nothing outside this group.

```wavedrom
  { "name": "start",     "wave": "010........" },
  { "name": "work busy", "wave": "0.1......0." },
  { "name": "timer",     "wave": "0.=.....=..", "data": ["counting", "expired"] },
  { "name": "timed_out", "wave": "0.......1.." }
],
  "head": { "text": "timeout branch wins: work is killed, error reported" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
task automatic do_with_timeout(input time limit, output bit ok);
  bit done_flag = 0;
  fork begin                          // isolation wrapper
    fork
      begin                           // branch 1: real work
        drive_and_wait_response();    // user task
        done_flag = 1;
      end
      begin                           // branch 2: watchdog
        #(limit);
      end
    join_any
    disable fork;                     // kills only the two branches above
  end join
  ok = done_flag;
  if (!ok) begin
    `uvm_error("TIMEOUT", $sformatf("no response within %0t (state=%s)",
               limit, dump_state()))
    release_bus();                    // free semaphores, deassert valid, etc.
  end
endtask
```

### Explanation
- `join_any` returns at the first completion and leaves the other branch alive. You must clean it up.
- Without the outer `fork begin ... end join`, `disable fork` would also kill sibling threads spawned earlier by this process. Monitors forked in the same `run_phase` are a common victim.
- Use a flag to record which branch won. If the work finishes at exactly `limit`, both branches end in the same time step and the order is scheduler dependent. Fix the rule (for example, check `done_flag`, so a tie passes) or use `limit+1`.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- A killed work thread may leave a semaphore key taken or `valid` asserted. Always release protocol resources on timeout.
- Use a clock-cycle watchdog (`repeat (N) @(posedge clk)`) when the limit is defined in cycles. It does not depend on the timescale.
- Report useful state (outstanding IDs, FSM state), not just "timeout".

### Follow-ups
- *Why not `wait fork` after join_any?* That would wait for the timer, which defeats the timeout.
- *UVM alternative?* `phase.phase_done.set_drain_time`, or a `uvm_root` global timeout via `set_timeout` for the whole test.

**Key idea:** Non-blocking assignments sample every RHS first and update later, so `a<=b; b<=a;` swaps the two values. Blocking assignments update immediately: after `a=b;`, the next line `b=a;` reads the new `a`, so both end up holding the old `b`.

| Code (old a=3, b=5) | after stmt 1 | after stmt 2 | final a,b | Swap? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `a <= b; b <= a;` | a scheduled ←5 | b scheduled ←3 | 5, 3 | yes |
| `a = b; b = a;` | a=5 | b=a=5 | 5, 5 | no |
| `t = a; a = b; b = t;` | t=3 | a=5 | 5, 3 | yes |
| `{a, b} = {b, a};` | RHS concatenation evaluated once | – | 5, 3 | yes |
| `a = a ^ b; b = a ^ b; a = a ^ b;` | a=6 | b=3 | 5, 3 | yes (unless a and b alias) |

```wavedrom

  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p..." },
  { "name": "a (NBA swap)", "wave": "=.==", "data": ["3", "5", "3"] },
  { "name": "b (NBA swap)", "wave": "=.==", "data": ["5", "3", "5"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "always_ff with a<=b; b<=a; swaps on every edge" } }
```

### Explanation
- NBA: the RHS is evaluated in the Active region and the LHS is updated in the NBA region, after every process triggered by that edge has read the old values.
- Blocking swaps without a temp: use the concatenation `{a,b} = {b,a}` (clean and synthesizable) or XOR/add-subtract tricks (they only work on integral values and look obscure).
- For `{a,b}={b,a}` the widths of a and b must match their positions. Each side is one packed vector.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The XOR swap zeroes the value if both names refer to the same storage (`a[i]`, `a[j]` with i==j).
- Using blocking assignments in clocked logic that another `always` block reads creates a race.
- Mixing `=` and `<=` to the same variable is illegal in `always_ff` and a lint error in general.

### Follow-ups
- *Swap in one always_comb?* `{a_n, b_n} = {b, a};`. Combinational logic is just wiring.
- *Swap with arithmetic?* `a=a+b; b=a-b; a=a-b;`. Overflow wraps, so it still works modulo 2^N.

| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 | inner B finishes → inner join_any releases | `B @5`, `D @5` |
| 10 | outer branch 1 finishes → **outer join_any releases** | `A @10`, `F @10` |
| 13 | branch 2 (still alive) wakes | `H @13` |

**Key idea:** Pick the join type from the completion rule you need: `join` waits for all branches, `join_any` waits for the first, and `join_none` waits for none, so you coordinate later with `wait fork` or events. Run a watchdog in parallel, and keep it inside its own isolated fork so killing it cannot hurt other threads.

| Construct | Parent continues when | Remaining children |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fork ... join` | all branches finish | none left |
| `fork ... join_any` | first branch finishes | keep running |
| `fork ... join_none` | immediately (children start when parent blocks) | all running |

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  TEST["main_phase: raise objection"] --> F["fork (isolated)"]
  F --> W1["traffic seq A"]
  F --> W2["traffic seq B"]
  F --> WD["watchdog: #MAX or N cycles"]
  W1 --> J{"join_any of (all work) vs watchdog"}
  W2 --> J
  WD --> J
  J -->|work first| OK["disable fork, pass"]
  J -->|watchdog first| ERR["uvm_fatal with state dump"]
  OK --> DROP["drop objection"]
  ERR --> DROP
```

### Code
```systemverilog
task main_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this);
  fork begin                                  // isolation wrapper
    fork
      begin : all_work
        fork                                  // all traffic must complete
          seq_a.start(env.agt_a.sqr);
          seq_b.start(env.agt_b.sqr);
        join
      end
      begin : watchdog
        repeat (cfg.max_cycles) @(posedge vif.clk);
        `uvm_fatal("WDOG", $sformatf("hang: a_sent=%0d b_sent=%0d",
                   seq_a.sent, seq_b.sent))
      end
    join_any
    disable fork;                             // kill watchdog (or stuck work)
  end join
  phase.drop_objection(this);
endtask
```

### Explanation
- The inner `fork...join` expresses "both sequences done". The middle `join_any` races that against the watchdog.
- `disable fork` inside the wrapper affects only these branches. Monitors forked elsewhere survive.
- Count the watchdog in clock cycles, not `#time`, so it scales with the clock period. Also check a global `uvm_root::set_timeout` as a last resort.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Raising the objection after the fork, or in a forked child, can let the phase end at time 0.
- The `join_none` loop variable capture bug: use `automatic int j = i;` in each iteration.
- A watchdog that fires should dump outstanding transactions and FSM states, not just say "timeout".

### Follow-ups
- *What does `wait fork` wait for?* All child processes of the current process, including ones forked earlier.
- *Why not `disable watchdog`?* A named-block disable affects every activation of that block. Process handles or an isolated fork are safer.

**Key idea:** At each clock edge, run the blocking statements in source order and update them immediately. For each NBA, record the RHS value at the moment its line executes. The NBA updates are applied all together after the block finishes. A table of *old state → sampled values → new state* per edge makes the analysis mechanical.

### Example
```systemverilog

  a  = b;        // blocking: a updates now
  b <= a + 1;    // NBA: RHS uses NEW a
  c  = b;        // blocking: reads OLD b (NBA not applied yet)
  d <= c + a;    // NBA: uses new c and new a
end
// initial: a=0 b=1 c=0 d=0
```

| 1 | 0,1,0,0 | a=1 | 2 | c=1 | 2 | 1,2,1,2 |
| 2 | 1,2,1,2 | a=2 | 3 | c=2 | 4 | 2,3,2,4 |

**Key idea:** `disable <name>` stops **every** active activation of that named block, and `disable fork` stops **all** children of the current process. To stop one branch selectively, save a `process` handle per branch and `kill()` only that one. If you must use `disable fork`, put each group under its own wrapper process so the disable is scoped to that group.

```mermaid

  P["parent process"] --> G1["wrapper group 1"]
  P --> G2["wrapper group 2"]
  G1 --> A["task A"]
  G1 --> B["task B"]
  G2 --> C["task C"]
  G2 --> D["task D"]
  X["disable fork inside group 1"] -.->|kills| A
  X -.->|kills| B
  Y["hB.kill()"] -.->|kills only| B
```

```systemverilog
module tb;
  process hA, hB;

  initial begin
    // Group 1: selective kill with handles
    fork
      begin hA = process::self(); forever #5  $display("%0t A", $time); end
      begin hB = process::self(); forever #7  $display("%0t B", $time); end
    join_none

    // Group 2: wrapper, so disable fork only reaches C and D
    fork begin
      fork
        begin #30 $display("%0t C done", $time); end
        begin #50 $display("%0t D done", $time); end
      join_any
      disable fork;                 // kills D only (it is the only survivor)
    end join_none

    wait (hA != null && hB != null);
    #20 hB.kill();                  // B stops, A continues
    #20 hA.kill();
  end
endmodule
```

| --- | --- | --- |
| `disable blk_name` | all activations of the named block | static name; hits other calls of the same task |
| `disable fork` | all descendants of the calling process | kills unrelated earlier forks unless wrapped |
| `process::kill()` | one process (and its children) | need handle; null until branch starts |

**Key idea:** Every `join_none` child starts only after the parent blocks. By then a shared loop variable has already reached its final value, so each child must capture its own copy in an `automatic` variable. Any other variable shared by children that write it in the same time step is a race, because the result depends on scheduling. Use a mailbox or semaphore when the order matters.

### Code
```systemverilog
module tb;
  int x;

  initial begin
    // ---- Part 1: buggy capture ----
    x = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
      fork
        begin #(i) x += i; $display("BUG t=%0t i=%0d x=%0d", $time, i, x); end
      join_none
    wait fork;

    // ---- Part 2: correct capture ----
    x = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) begin
      automatic int j = i;              // evaluated per iteration
      fork
        begin #(j) x += j; $display("OK  t=%0t j=%0d x=%0d", $time, j, x); end
      join_none
    end
    wait fork;

    // ---- Part 3: join_any + race ----
    x = 0;
    fork
      #5 x = 10;
      #5 x = 20;
      #2 x = 30;
    join_any
    $display("after join_any t=%0t x=%0d", $time, x);  // t=2 x=30
    #3 $display("t=%0t x=%0d (10 or 20!)", $time, x);  // race
  end
endmodule
```

### Trace
| Part | time | child sees | x after | why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3 | i=3 | 3 | loop finished (i=3) before any child ran |
| 1 | 3 | i=3 | 6 | |
| 1 | 3 | i=3 | 9 | all three wait `#3` |
| 2 | 3 (+0) | j=0 | 0 | own copy |
| 2 | 4 (+1) | j=1 | 1 | |
| 2 | 5 (+2) | j=2 | 3 | |
| 3 | 5 | – | 30 then 10 or 20 | two writers in same timestep |

(Part 2 starts at t=3 because Part 1's `wait fork` returns at t=3.)

### Explanation
- In Part 1, the `for` variable `i` is a single variable in the loop scope. The children read it when they wake, not when they were forked.
- `automatic int j = i;` in the loop body makes a new variable per iteration, and the fork captures it.
- In Part 3, both `#5` writers wake in the same Active region, and the LRM does not order them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Declaring `automatic` inside the `fork` block before `begin` also works, because declarations in a fork initialize when the fork executes.
- `wait fork` waits for *all* children of the process, including earlier unrelated ones.
- A semaphore protects a read-modify-write such as `x += j` from interleaving across a delay, but it does not choose which child goes first.

- *Make Part 3 deterministic?* Have the writers `put` into a mailbox and let a single consumer apply the values in arrival order, or give them different delays.

**Key idea:** The *handle type* decides which members you may access and which **non-virtual** method runs. The *object type* decides which **virtual** method runs. Upcasting (derived → base handle) is implicit and always safe. Downcasting needs `$cast`, which checks the object's runtime type. No cast ever changes the object itself.

```mermaid
classDiagram
  class Packet {
    +int addr
    +display() virtual
    +id() non-virtual
  }
  class EthPacket {
    +int vlan
    +display()
    +id()
  }
  Packet <|-- EthPacket
```

### Code
```systemverilog
class Packet;
  int addr;
  virtual function void display(); $display("Packet addr=%0d", addr); endfunction
  function string id(); return "Packet"; endfunction
endclass

class EthPacket extends Packet;
  int vlan = 7;
  virtual function void display(); $display("Eth addr=%0d vlan=%0d", addr, vlan); endfunction
  function string id(); return "EthPacket"; endfunction
endclass

module tb;
  initial begin
    Packet    p;
    EthPacket e = new, e2;
    Packet    p_only = new;

    p = e;                       // upcast: implicit
    p.display();                 // Eth addr=0 vlan=7   (virtual -> object type)
    $display(p.id());            // Packet               (non-virtual -> handle type)
    // p.vlan = 1;               // compile error: not a member of Packet

    if ($cast(e2, p)) e2.vlan = 3;     // succeeds: object is EthPacket
    if (!$cast(e2, p_only))            // fails: object is plain Packet
      $display("downcast failed, e2 unchanged");
  end
endmodule
```

| Call | Handle type | Object type | Runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `p.display()` | Packet | EthPacket | `EthPacket::display` |
| `p.id()` | Packet | EthPacket | `Packet::id` |
| `$cast(e2, p)` | – | EthPacket | success |
| `$cast(e2, p_only)` | – | Packet | returns 0 |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `e2 = p;` without `$cast` is a compile error. When `$cast` is called as a task and fails, it is a runtime error, so call it as a function and check the return value.
- Once a method is declared `virtual` in a base class, overrides are virtual automatically. The prototype must match exactly.
- `super.display()` inside the derived method calls the base implementation explicitly.

### Follow-ups
- *Where does UVM rely on this?* `uvm_sequence_item` handles in the driver, `do_copy`/`do_compare` overrides, and factory overrides all depend on virtual dispatch.

**Key idea:** Wrap every loop iteration in its own `fork begin ... end join_none` process, and give it an `automatic` copy of the loop index plus its own semaphore or event. Each group can then wait, block, or `disable fork` inside its own wrapper without touching the other groups. A global `wait fork` or `disable fork` in the parent would hit every group at once.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  P["parent: for g in 0..N-1"] --> W0["wrapper g=0"]
  P --> W1["wrapper g=1"]
  P --> W2["wrapper g=2"]
  W0 --> T00["task(0,a)"]
  W0 --> T01["task(0,b)"]
  W1 --> T10["task(1,a)"]
  W1 --> T11["task(1,b)"]
  W2 --> T20["task(2,a)"]
  W2 --> T21["task(2,b)"]
  GATE["gate[1].get() blocks"] -.->|"only group 1 waits"| W1
```

### Code
```systemverilog
module tb;
  localparam int N = 3;
  semaphore gate[N];
  event     grp_done[N];
  process   grp_h[N];

  task automatic work(int g, string tag, int d);
    #d $display("%0t grp%0d %s", $time, g, tag);
  endtask

  initial begin
    foreach (gate[i]) gate[i] = new(1);

    for (int g = 0; g < N; g++) begin
      automatic int gid = g;               // per-iteration copy
      fork begin                           // wrapper process for this group
        grp_h[gid] = process::self();
        gate[gid].get(1);                  // blocks only this group
        fork                               // children local to this wrapper
          work(gid, "a", 5 + gid);
          work(gid, "b", 2 * gid + 1);
        join                               // or join_any + disable fork (scoped)
        gate[gid].put(1);
        -> grp_done[gid];
      end join_none
    end

    // Example: hold group 1 by taking its key before it runs
    gate[1].get(1);
    #20 gate[1].put(1);                    // group 1 starts at t=20

    wait (grp_done[0].triggered);          // wait for one group only
    $display("%0t group 0 finished, others unaffected", $time);
    wait fork;                             // finally wait for all
  end
endmodule
```

### Explanation
- `automatic int gid = g;` in the loop body is evaluated per iteration, so every wrapper sees its own index.
- Inside a wrapper, `disable fork` and `wait fork` see only that wrapper's children.
- Per-group semaphores or events give per-group control. One global semaphore would serialize every group.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- In the code above the parent takes `gate[1]` before the children run (they start only when the parent blocks), so group 1 is held. If the parent took it later, the outcome would depend on timing.
- `@grp_done[i]` can miss an event triggered earlier in the same timestep. `wait(ev.triggered)` is safer within that timestep, or use a mailbox or flag.
- Keep `process` handles if you need to kill one group: `grp_h[2].kill()`.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not one `fork ... join_none` containing all tasks?* Then there is no group boundary, and any `disable fork` kills everything.

**Key idea:** In SVA, `|->` (overlapping) starts checking the consequent in the **same** clock tick in which the antecedent matched. `|=>` (non-overlapping) starts it one tick **later**. So `a |=> b` is exactly `a |-> ##1 b`. With a multi-cycle antecedent, the consequent is anchored at the antecedent's **last** cycle. A bare `->` is something else: implication in constraints, or an event trigger.

```wavedrom

  { "name": "clk", "wave": "p......." },
  { "name": "req", "wave": "010.10.." },
  { "name": "ack", "wave": "010..10." },
  { "name": "req |-> ack", "wave": "x=x.=x..", "data": ["pass", "FAIL"] },
  { "name": "req |=> ack", "wave": "x.=x.=x.", "data": ["FAIL", "pass"] }
],
  "head": { "text": "result shown at the tick where the consequent is evaluated" } }
```

### Code
```systemverilog
// overlapping: ack must be high in the same cycle as req
a_ovl:  assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |-> ack);

// non-overlapping: ack one cycle after req (same as req |-> ##1 ack)
a_novl: assert property (@(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n) req |=> ack);

// multi-cycle antecedent: consequent starts where "start ##1 go" ends
a_seq:  assert property (@(posedge clk) start ##1 go |-> ##[1:3] done);

// other meanings of "->"
constraint c_len { (kind == SHORT) -> (len < 16); }   // constraint implication
initial -> ev_start;                                    // trigger named event
```

### Explanation
| Operator | Context | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `A \|-> B` | property | if A matches at tick t, B must match starting at t |
| `A \|=> B` | property | if A matches at tick t, B must match starting at t+1 |
| `A -> B` | constraint / expression | logical implication (`!A \|\| B`) |
| `-> ev` | procedural | trigger event `ev` |

- If the antecedent does not match, the property passes **vacuously**. Add a `cover property (req)` so you know the check actually ran.
- When the antecedent is a sequence with several possible match points (`a ##[1:3] b`), each match starts its own consequent thread.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `$rose(req) |=> ack` vs `req |=> ack`: with level-sensitive `req` held high, the second form starts a new check every cycle.
- `|->` with a consequent that is only `##0` is the same tick. Mixing up the two operators gives a one-cycle-off checker that fails on every legal transaction.
- Sampled values: both sides use values from the Preponed region, so the check sees what the flops saw.

### Follow-ups
- *Write "ack within 1–4 cycles after req":* `req |=> ##[0:3] ack`, or equivalently `req |-> ##[1:4] ack`.

| Use a virtual class when... | Prefer something else when... |
| --- | --- |
| a base object is meaningless (generic "transaction", "shape", "codec") | the base itself is a sensible default → concrete base class with virtual methods |
| every subtype **must** implement a method (compile-time enforcement) | you only need a method set shared by unrelated hierarchies → `interface class` + `implements` |

- UVM factory registration works for concrete subclasses. An abstract class should not be registered with `` `uvm_object_utils `` because `create` would try to `new` it.

**Key idea:** C++ passes pointers **by value**. A function can change the pointed-to data through its copy, but reassigning the copy never changes the caller's pointer. To swap the caller's pointers, take `T*&` (reference to pointer) or `T**`. In `const T* p` the data is read-only (pointer to const). In `T* const p` the pointer itself cannot be reseated (const pointer).

### Code
```cpp
#include <iostream>

void swap_by_value(int* a, int* b) { int* t = a; a = b; b = t; }      // no effect
void swap_by_ref  (int*& a, int*& b) { int* t = a; a = b; b = t; }    // swaps caller ptrs
void swap_by_pp   (int** a, int** b) { int* t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }// swaps caller ptrs
void swap_values  (int* a, int* b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }   // swaps the ints

int main() {
  int x = 1, y = 2;
  int *px = &x, *py = &y;

  swap_by_value(px, py); std::cout << *px << *py << "\n";  // 12
  swap_by_ref(px, py);   std::cout << *px << *py << "\n";  // 21 (px->y)
  swap_by_pp(&px, &py);  std::cout << *px << *py << "\n";  // 12 (back)
  swap_values(px, py);   std::cout << x << y << "\n";      // 21 (x,y changed)

  const int* pc = &x;   // pointer to const
  // *pc = 5;           // error: data read-only through pc
  pc = &y;              // ok: can reseat

  int* const cp = &x;   // const pointer
  *cp = 5;              // ok: data writable
  // cp = &y;           // error: cannot reseat

  const int* const cc = &x;  // both fixed
  (void)cc;
}
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Caller
    PX["px"] --> X["x=1"]
    PY["py"] --> Y["y=2"]
  end
  subgraph swap_by_value
    A["a (copy of px)"] --> X
    B["b (copy of py)"] --> Y
  end
  NOTE["swapping a,b changes only the copies"]
```

| Declaration | Change `*p`? | Change `p`? | Read right-to-left |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `const int* p` / `int const* p` | no | yes | p is pointer to const int |
| `int* const p` | yes | no | p is const pointer to int |
| `const int* const p` | no | no | const pointer to const int |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `std::swap(px, py)` already does this generically (it takes references).
- A reference to pointer cannot bind to a temporary (`swap_by_ref(&x, &y)` fails), but `swap_by_pp` would need `&px`.
- Casting away const and then writing to an object that is really const is undefined behavior.

### Follow-ups
- *SystemVerilog analog?* Class handles are passed by value too. Use `ref` arguments to reseat the caller's handle.
tongxin-205:
**Key idea:** UVM buys **reuse and scalability**: standard agents, sequences, factory overrides, configuration, TLM, phasing, reporting and RAL let large teams share and reconfigure testbenches across blocks and projects. The price is boilerplate, a learning curve, simulation overhead and harder debugging of framework internals. A small one-off block test may be cheaper as a plain self-checking SV testbench.

| UVM feature | Benefit | Cost / risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agents (drv/mon/sqr) | plug-and-play VIP, active/passive reuse block → SoC | many classes even for a trivial interface |
| Sequences, virtual sequences | layered, constrained-random scenarios | sequencer arbitration and handshake to learn |
| Factory | swap drivers/items per test without edits | type registration everywhere; `new` bypasses it |
| config_db | hierarchical configuration | string paths fail silently on typos; slow if overused |
| TLM / analysis ports | decoupled components, multiple subscribers | indirection makes data flow harder to trace |
| Phases + objections | standard build/connect/run/check order | hangs and early exits from objection mistakes |
| Reporting | severity, verbosity, IDs, catchers | log volume |
| RAL | register access by name, mirror, built-in tests | model generation and adapter/predictor setup |
| Standard (IEEE 1800.2) | common skills, vendor VIP | version quirks (UVM 1.1d vs 1.2 vs 2020) |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q{"block size / lifetime?"} -->|"small, one-off, simple I/O"| SIMPLE["self-checking SV TB"]
  Q -->|"reused, multi-interface, team"| UVM["UVM env with agents"]
  UVM --> REUSE["reuse at subsystem/SoC level"]
```

### Explanation
- The real payoff comes on the second and third projects: agents and sequences move from block to subsystem to SoC, and passive agents become monitors.
- Tests stay small. They configure and override instead of copying the environment.
- Costs are mostly upfront: templates and code generators lower them, and team conventions keep config_db and factory use disciplined.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Over-engineering: a 50-line combinational block does not need a full agent.
- Performance: heavy field macros, `uvm_config_db` lookups in hot loops and verbose `sprint` calls slow regressions.
- Debug: use `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE`, `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE`, `factory.print()` and `uvm_top.print_topology()`.

### Follow-ups
- *Is UVM required for formal or emulation?* No. Formal uses properties, and emulation often uses transaction-level, synthesizable transactors (SCE-MI) with UVM running only on the host side.

**Key idea:** Every component's `run_phase` starts in parallel, and their relative start order is not something to rely on. The phase stays alive only while the total objection count is above zero. Dropping *your* objection ends nothing if others are still raised. When the count reaches zero (after any drain time), UVM **kills** all remaining `run_phase` threads, including `forever` loops in monitors and drivers, and moves on to extract, check and report.

```wavedrom
  { "name": "total count",    "wave": "=.=.=..==.", "data": ["0", "1", "2", "1", "0"] },
```

```systemverilog
class my_test extends base_test;
  `uvm_component_utils(my_test)
  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction

  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    my_seq seq = my_seq::type_id::create("seq");
    phase.raise_objection(this, "main traffic");     // at time 0, before any #delay
    phase.phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 200ns);     // let last responses drain
    seq.start(env.agt.sqr);
    phase.drop_objection(this, "main traffic");
  endtask
endclass

class my_scoreboard extends uvm_scoreboard;
  // raise while expectations are pending, drop when queue empties
  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    forever begin
      @(pending_changed);
      if (exp_q.size() && !raised) begin phase.raise_objection(this); raised = 1; end
      if (!exp_q.size() && raised) begin phase.drop_objection(this); raised = 0; end
    end
  endtask
endclass
```

### Explanation
- Raise at time 0. If no objection is raised before the first nonblocking assignment / delta settles, the run phase ends immediately and the test "passes" with zero traffic.
- Objections propagate up the hierarchy (`uvm_test_top` keeps the total). `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE` prints every raise and drop.
- With the run-time sub-phases (reset/configure/main/shutdown), each sub-phase has its own objections. `run_phase` runs in parallel with all of them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Monitors and drivers should not raise objections in their `forever` loops, or the test never ends.
- Code after `drop_objection` in the same task may never execute, because the thread can be killed.
- Raising in a component that has already dropped is fine. The count simply goes back up.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you end a test that hangs?* Use `uvm_top.set_timeout(…)` or `+UVM_TIMEOUT`, plus a watchdog with a state dump.

**Key idea:** **Function phases** (build, connect, end_of_elaboration, start_of_simulation, extract, check, report, final) are `function void` methods, so they cannot consume simulation time. Most other function phases run bottom-up.

| Time | zero; no `#`, `@`, `wait` | consumes time |
| Order across components | sequential (top-down or bottom-up traversal) | all components run in parallel |
| Ends when | function returns | all objections dropped (+ drain time) |
| Typical content | create, connect, print topology, final checks | drive/monitor traffic, start sequences |

### Explanation
- Top-down build lets a parent set config and overrides before the child calls `create`.
- Bottom-up connect and check mean children are fully wired or checked before the parent that uses them.
- `run_phase` runs concurrently with the 12 runtime sub-phases. Use one model or the other per component, and avoid mixing objections across them.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Calling a time-consuming task from `build_phase` is a compile error, or a fatal if done via `fork`.
- Creating a component outside `build_phase` (for example in `run_phase`) is illegal. The hierarchy is frozen after build.
- `final_phase` runs top-down, the exception among the cleanup phases.

### Follow-ups
- *Can you jump phases?* Yes, `phase.jump(uvm_reset_phase::get())` for a mid-test reset, but only among the runtime phases.

**Key idea:** Pick the primitive by what must be passed: **mailbox / `uvm_tlm_fifo`** for queued data (nothing is lost if the consumer is slow), **semaphore** for mutual exclusion or counting resources, and **event / `uvm_event` / `uvm_barrier`** for pure "it happened" signalling. A queued token survives a "notify before wait" race. A raw `@event` is missed if it fires before the waiter arrives.

| Primitive | Carries data | Remembers past notify | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `mailbox #(T)` | yes, FIFO | yes (queued) | generator → driver, monitor → checker |
| `uvm_tlm_fifo` / `uvm_tlm_analysis_fifo` | yes | yes | scoreboard input buffering |
| `semaphore` | no (keys) | yes (key count) | shared bus, memory model lock |
| `event` with `@ev` | no | no, edge only | same-time handshake |
| `event` with `wait(ev.triggered)` | no | only within the same timestep | avoids same-timestep race |
| `uvm_event` | optional object | `wait_ptrigger` persistent until reset | cross-component notify via pool |
| `uvm_barrier` | no | counts arrivals | N threads meet before proceeding |

```systemverilog
    repeat (6) begin mb.get(v); $display("%0t got %0d", $time, v); #2; end
```

**Key idea:** Code coverage measures how much of the **RTL structure** the tests executed. The tool collects it automatically: statement/line, branch, condition/expression, toggle and FSM state/transition. Functional coverage measures whether the **planned behaviors** occurred, and you write it yourself as covergroups or cover properties. Neither one proves correctness, because checkers must actually observe the result.

### Example: what each metric asks
```systemverilog
module arb (input logic clk, rst_n, a, b, output logic gnt_a, gnt_b);
  typedef enum logic [1:0] {IDLE, GA, GB} st_e;
  st_e st;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n) begin
    if (!rst_n)                 st <= IDLE;          // line / statement
    else if (a && !b)           st <= GA;            // branch + condition (a, !b)
    else if (b)                 st <= GB;            // branch
    else                        st <= IDLE;          // branch (else)
  end
  assign gnt_a = (st == GA);                         // toggle on gnt_a 0->1, 1->0
  assign gnt_b = (st == GB);
endmodule
```

| Metric | Hole example in `arb` | Test needed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Statement/line | `st <= GB` never executed | drive `b=1` |
| Branch | final `else` never taken | `a=0, b=0` after reset |
| Condition / expression (FEC/MC/DC) | `a && !b` never false due to `!b` alone | `a=1, b=1` |
| Toggle | `gnt_b` never went 1→0 | grant B then release |
| FSM state | `GB` never reached | as above |
| FSM transition | `GA → GB` never seen | `a` then `b` together |
| Functional (user-written) | "B wins when both request" never sampled | covergroup cross `a × b × gnt` |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  PLAN["verification plan"] --> FC["functional coverage (covergroups, cover property)"]
  RTL["RTL"] --> CC["code coverage (tool-generated)"]
  FC --> SIGNOFF{"both closed + all checks pass"}
  CC --> SIGNOFF
```

### Explanation
- Enable it with tool switches, for example VCS `-cm line+cond+branch+tgl+fsm` or Xcelium `-coverage all`, then merge the databases from the regression.
- 100% code coverage with missing features is possible because code coverage cannot see what is *not* implemented. 100% functional coverage with dead RTL is also possible. Review the holes in both.
- Use exclusions (with reviewed justification) for unreachable code: tie-offs, defensive `default` branches, parameters not used in this config.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Expression coverage is reported per operand, and short-circuit operators can make some terms impossible to cover alone.
- Toggle coverage on wide buses can be noisy. Restrict it to ports or control signals.
- Coverage collected while a checker is disabled shows lines that ran without being checked.

### Follow-ups
- *What is assertion coverage?* Cover properties and assertion pass counts (non-vacuous) show the temporal behaviors that were actually checked.

**Key idea:** A byte-enable (strobe) write must update **only** the enabled byte lanes of the reference memory. For each lane `i` with `strb[i]==1`, set `mem[beat_addr + i] = data[8*i +: 8]`, and leave the other bytes unchanged. The common bug is writing the whole word, which corrupts the disabled bytes in the model, so a later read "mismatches" against a correct DUT.

### Worked example (32-bit bus, little-endian)
| Step | Address 0x100 bytes [3:0] | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| initial | `44 33 22 11` | word 0x44332211 |
| write data=0xAABBCCDD, strb=0b0101 | `44 BB 22 DD` | lanes 0 and 2 only |
| buggy model (ignores strb) | `AA BB CC DD` | wrong: lanes 1 and 3 overwritten |
| read 0x100 | DUT returns 0x44BB22DD | buggy SB flags a false error |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  D["data AA BB CC DD"] --> L0{"strb0=1"}
  D --> L1{"strb1=0"}
  D --> L2{"strb2=1"}
  D --> L3{"strb3=0"}
  L0 -->|"DD"| M0["mem[0x100]"]
  L2 -->|"BB"| M2["mem[0x102]"]
  L1 -.->|keep 22| M1["mem[0x101]"]
  L3 -.->|keep 44| M3["mem[0x103]"]
```

```systemverilog
class mem_scoreboard extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(mem_scoreboard)
  uvm_analysis_imp #(bus_tr, mem_scoreboard) imp;
  localparam int NB = 4;                      // bytes per beat (data width / 8)
  bit [7:0] ref_mem [bit [31:0]];             // byte-addressed
  bit       big_endian = 0;

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent); imp = new("imp", this);
  endfunction

  // lane i of the bus carries byte (aligned_addr + i) in little-endian
  function int lane_to_offset(int i); return big_endian ? NB - 1 - i : i; endfunction

  function void write(bus_tr t);
    bit [31:0] base = t.addr & ~(NB - 1);     // beat-aligned address
    if (t.is_write) begin
      for (int i = 0; i < NB; i++)
        if (t.strb[i])                        // FIX: only enabled lanes
          ref_mem[base + lane_to_offset(i)] = t.wdata[8*i +: 8];
    end else begin
      for (int i = 0; i < NB; i++) begin
        bit [31:0] a = base + lane_to_offset(i);
        bit [7:0]  exp = ref_mem.exists(a) ? ref_mem[a] : 8'h00;  // define default
        if (t.rdata[8*i +: 8] !== exp)
          `uvm_error("RD", $sformatf("addr %h lane %0d exp %h got %h",
                     a, i, exp, t.rdata[8*i +: 8]))
      end
    end
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Explanation
- Storing bytes, not words, makes partial writes, unaligned addresses and different bus widths straightforward.
- For a burst, compute each beat's address (INCR/WRAP/FIXED) and apply that beat's strobe. With narrow transfers, only the lanes of the active byte slice are valid.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `strb == 0`: a legal no-op write. The model must not change and must not report an error.
- `strb == '1`: full word write.
- Overlapping masked writes to the same word in a row: each write updates only its own lanes.
- Reads of bytes never written: define the expected value (reset value, X or "don't check"). Do not silently pass.

### Follow-ups
- *Sub-word reads?* Compare only the requested byte lanes, i.e. those derived from address and size.

**Key idea:** The model's write order must match the **DUT's commit order** as defined by the spec, not the order in which monitor callbacks happen to fire. Drive all updates through a single ordered path, for example timestamp plus a defined priority, or the arbiter's grant observed by a monitor. When two writes overlap in the same cycle, apply the specified priority per byte. A semaphore or single thread only prevents torn updates. It cannot tell you which write should win.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  M0["port 0 monitor"] -->|"wr, cycle"| ORD["ordering stage: sort by (cycle, priority) or by observed grant"]
  M1["port 1 monitor"] -->|"wr, cycle"| ORD
  M2["port 2 monitor"] -->|"wr, cycle"| ORD
  ORD --> MEM["sparse ref memory (single writer)"]
  RD["read monitor"] --> CHK["compare vs MEM"]
  MEM --> CHK
```

### Same-cycle overlap example (port 0 has priority)
| Byte addr | Port 0 (strb) | Port 1 (strb) | Model result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0x10 | AA (1) | 11 (1) | AA (p0 wins) |
| 0x11 | BB (0) | 22 (1) | 22 (only p1 enabled) |
| 0x12 | CC (1) | 33 (0) | CC |

```systemverilog
class mem_model extends uvm_component;
  `uvm_component_utils(mem_model)
  bit [7:0] mem [bit [63:0]];
  wr_tr pending[$];                    // writes of the current cycle
  longint cur_cycle = -1;

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent); super.new(name, parent); endfunction

  // called by every port monitor (any order within a cycle)
  function void add_write(wr_tr t);
    if (t.cycle != cur_cycle) commit();  // new cycle: flush previous
    cur_cycle = t.cycle;
    pending.push_back(t);
  endfunction

  // apply lowest priority first so the highest priority overwrites last
  function void commit();
    pending.sort(x) with (-x.port_priority);   // descending number = lower priority first
    foreach (pending[i])
      foreach (pending[i].strb[b])
        if (pending[i].strb[b]) mem[pending[i].addr + b] = pending[i].data[8*b +: 8];
    pending.delete();
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Explanation
- If arbitration is internal and unspecified, monitor the arbiter's grant or memory-array write port (white box) and apply writes in that order.
- Interconnects with outstanding transactions: order by the point of **completion/commit** (e.g. write response), as the memory-ordering rules define.
- Read-vs-write in the same cycle: the spec decides read-old or read-new, and the model must implement the same rule.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Commit the last cycle at end of test, or before checking a read in a later cycle.
- Non-deterministic legal outcomes (no priority defined): accept any of the legal values and record which ones were allowed.
- Monitors running in different clock domains need a common timestamp ($realtime) to order writes.

### Follow-ups
- *Why not lock with a semaphore?* It serializes access in callback order, which is arbitrary, so the model could still hold the wrong final byte.

**Key idea:** UVM phases are a fixed **schedule of callbacks** that every component implements as needed: build → connect → elaboration checks → run (time-consuming) → extract → check → report → final. A phase scheduler (`uvm_phase` graph, driven by `uvm_root` after `run_test()`) walks the graph. It calls function phases across the hierarchy in a defined traversal order, and it forks all components' task phases in parallel, waiting on objections.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Build["build-time (functions, 0 time)"]
    B["build (top-down)"] --> C["connect"] --> EOE["end_of_elaboration"] --> SOS["start_of_simulation"]
  end
  subgraph Run["run-time (tasks)"]
    RUN["run_phase"]
    PR["pre_reset .. post_shutdown (12 sub-phases)"]
  end
  subgraph Clean["cleanup (functions, 0 time)"]
    EX["extract"] --> CK["check"] --> RP["report"] --> FI["final"]
  end
  SOS --> RUN
  SOS --> PR
  RUN --> EX
  PR --> EX
```

### How it works
| Step | Mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| `run_test()` | creates `uvm_test_top` via factory, starts the phase graph |
| function phase | scheduler traverses the hierarchy (build top-down, others bottom-up) calling `xxx_phase(phase)` |
| task phase | scheduler forks `run_phase` of every component at once |
| phase end | when the objection count reaches 0 (+ drain time), remaining task threads are killed |
| sync | all components are in the same runtime sub-phase by default (domains can unsync) |
| jump | `phase.jump()` can go back, e.g. to reset |

**Key idea:** An objection is a **reference count of "work still in progress"** attached to a task phase. A component raises it before starting work that must finish and drops it afterwards. Counts propagate up the hierarchy to `uvm_test_top`. When the total reaches zero, the phase waits out its drain time and then ends, killing every leftover thread in that phase.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant T as test
  participant S as scoreboard
  participant P as phase (count)
  T->>P: raise (count 1)
  T->>T: seq.start()
  S->>P: raise while expected queue non-empty (count 2)
  T->>P: drop (count 1)
  S->>P: drop when queue empty (count 0)
  P->>P: drain time elapses
  P-->>T: phase ends, kill run_phase threads
```

### Code
```systemverilog
task main_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  phase.raise_objection(this, "traffic");
  vseq.start(env.vsqr);
  phase.drop_objection(this, "traffic");
endtask

function void end_of_elaboration_phase(uvm_phase phase);
  uvm_phase mp = phase.find_by_name("main", 0);
  mp.phase_done.set_drain_time(this, 500ns);       // let pipeline flush
endfunction

// Optional: end-of-test vote, e.g. scoreboard delays ending while pending
virtual task phase_ready_to_end(uvm_phase phase);  // uvm_component callback
  if (phase.get_name() == "main" && exp_q.size()) begin
    phase.raise_objection(this, "pending");
    fork begin
      wait (exp_q.size() == 0);
      phase.drop_objection(this, "pending");
    end join_none
  end
endtask
```

### Explanation
- Raise objections in tests and sequences (scenario owners). Do not raise them in drivers or monitors, whose `forever` loops would never drop them.
- `+UVM_OBJECTION_TRACE` prints every raise and drop with its count, which is the first thing to check when a test ends at 0 ns or hangs.
- In a sequence, use `starting_phase` (UVM 1.1) or `get_starting_phase()` together with `set_automatic_phase_objection(1)` (UVM 1.2).

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Raise **before** the first time-consuming statement. A `#1` before the raise lets the phase end at time 0.
- Unbalanced raise/drop (an error path that returns early) causes a hang until the global timeout.
- Many raise/drop calls per transaction are slow. Use one objection per test or sequence, not per item.

### Follow-ups
- *Difference between drain time and phase_ready_to_end?* Drain time is a fixed delay after zero. `phase_ready_to_end` lets components re-raise conditionally.

**Key idea:** Keep one associative-array entry per **pair ID**, holding A's data, B's data, arrival times and seen flags. When a side arrives, check it is not a duplicate. If the other side is already present, compare and delete the entry. Otherwise store it and start the clock. A periodic sweep (or per-entry timer) reports any entry older than the timeout, and `check_phase` reports leftovers. Either side may arrive first.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  EMPTY --> HAVE_A: A arrives
  EMPTY --> HAVE_B: B arrives
  HAVE_A --> MATCHED: B arrives / compare
  HAVE_B --> MATCHED: A arrives / compare
  HAVE_A --> ERROR_DUP: A again
  HAVE_B --> ERROR_DUP: B again
  HAVE_A --> TIMEOUT: age > limit
  HAVE_B --> TIMEOUT: age > limit
  MATCHED --> EMPTY: delete entry
```

```systemverilog
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_a)
`uvm_analysis_imp_decl(_b)

class pair_sb extends uvm_scoreboard;
  `uvm_component_utils(pair_sb)
  uvm_analysis_imp_a #(pair_tr, pair_sb) a_imp;
  uvm_analysis_imp_b #(pair_tr, pair_sb) b_imp;

  typedef struct { pair_tr a, b; bit has_a, has_b; time t_first; } entry_t;
  entry_t tbl[int];                         // key: pair id
  time    timeout = 1us;
  int     n_match, n_err;

  function new(string name, uvm_component parent);
    super.new(name, parent);
    a_imp = new("a_imp", this); b_imp = new("b_imp", this);
  endfunction

  function void write_a(pair_tr t); arrive(t, 1); endfunction
  function void write_b(pair_tr t); arrive(t, 0); endfunction

  function void arrive(pair_tr t, bit is_a);
    entry_t e;
    if (tbl.exists(t.id)) e = tbl[t.id];
    else begin e.has_a = 0; e.has_b = 0; e.t_first = $time; end

    if (( is_a && e.has_a) || (!is_a && e.has_b)) begin       // duplicate
      `uvm_error("DUP", $sformatf("id %0d side %s duplicate", t.id, is_a ? "A" : "B"))
      n_err++; return;                                         // keep the original
    end
    if (is_a) begin e.a = t; e.has_a = 1; end
    else      begin e.b = t; e.has_b = 1; end

    if (e.has_a && e.has_b) begin                              // complete pair
      if (!e.a.compare(e.b)) begin
        `uvm_error("MISMATCH", $sformatf("id %0d A=%s B=%s", t.id,
                   e.a.convert2string(), e.b.convert2string())) n_err++;
      end else n_match++;
      tbl.delete(t.id);
    end else tbl[t.id] = e;
  endfunction

  task run_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    forever begin
      #(timeout / 4);                                          // sweep period
      foreach (tbl[id])
        if ($time - tbl[id].t_first > timeout) begin
          `uvm_error("TIMEOUT", $sformatf("id %0d only %s arrived at %0t", id,
                     tbl[id].has_a ? "A" : "B", tbl[id].t_first))
          tbl.delete(id); n_err++;                             // safe: foreach over keys copy
        end
    end
  endtask

  function void check_phase(uvm_phase phase);
    foreach (tbl[id]) `uvm_error("LEFTOVER", $sformatf("id %0d unpaired", id))
  endfunction
endclass
```

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Deleting from an associative array while iterating it with `foreach` is tool-dependent. The safest pattern collects expired keys into a queue first, then deletes them.
- A duplicate that arrives *after* its pair completed looks like a new first arrival. Keep a short "recently matched" set if the spec forbids it.
- With a sweep period of `timeout/4`, detection can be up to 25% late. Use per-entry `fork` timers if exact timing matters.
- The ID space can wrap: delete entries promptly and check on reuse.

### Follow-ups
- *Detect timeouts with no simulation time passing (zero-time)?* Not possible. Timeouts need a time base, either `#` or a clock count.

**Key idea:** Split on commas, strip whitespace, drop empty entries: `[x.strip() for x in text.split(',') if x.strip()]`. If names can contain quoted commas (`"Smith, John"`), use the `csv` module instead of `split`, because `split` is wrong for quoted fields.

### Code

```python
import csv
import io


def parse_names(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """'alice, bob,,carol ' -> ['alice', 'bob', 'carol']"""
    return [x.strip() for x in text.split(",") if x.strip()]


def parse_names_csv(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Handles quoted fields: 'a, "Smith, John", b' -> ['a', 'Smith, John', 'b']"""
    row = next(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text), skipinitialspace=True), [])
    return [x.strip() for x in row if x.strip()]


def parse_unique(text: str) -> list[str]:
    """Remove duplicates, keep first-seen order (dicts preserve insertion order)."""
    return list(dict.fromkeys(parse_names(text)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    assert parse_names("alice, bob,,carol ") == ["alice", "bob", "carol"]
    assert parse_names("") == []
    assert parse_names_csv('a, "Smith, John", b') == ["a", "Smith, John", "b"]
    assert parse_unique("a,b,a,c") == ["a", "b", "c"]
    print("ok")
```

| Input | `split(',')` | after strip + filter |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `"alice, bob,,carol "` | `['alice', ' bob', '', 'carol ']` | `['alice', 'bob', 'carol']` |
| `""` | `['']` | `[]` |
| `'a, "Smith, John"'` | `['a', ' "Smith', ' John"']` (wrong) | use `csv` → `['a', 'Smith, John']` |

- `"".split(',')` returns `['']`, not `[]`, which is why the filter is needed.
- `text.split()` with no argument splits on whitespace, which is a different behavior.
- Mixed separators (`;` or newlines): `re.split(r"[,;\n]", text)`.
- A list comprehension that calls `strip()` twice is fine for short inputs. For large inputs, use `filter(None, map(str.strip, text.split(',')))`.

```systemverilog
// full key path: "uvm_test_top.env.agt0.drv" + "max_delay"

// in tb_top (absolute path)
uvm_config_db #(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt*", "vif", bif);

// in driver::build_phase (cntxt = this, inst_name = "")
int d;
if (!uvm_config_db #(int)::get(this, "", "max_delay", d))
  `uvm_info("CFG", "using default delay", UVM_MEDIUM)
```

```mermaid
  GET["get(this=drv, '', 'max_delay', d)"] --> LOOK["lookup: uvm_test_top.env.agt0.drv / max_delay / int"]
  KEY --> MATCH{"match"}
  LOOK --> MATCH
```

### Precedence rules
- During build, a `set` from a **higher** component in the hierarchy wins over a `set` from a lower one (a test can override env defaults).
- At the same level, or after build, the **last** `set` wins.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- `int` vs `int unsigned` vs `bit [31:0]` are different `T`, so `get` misses silently.
- `get` must happen after the `set`. A child's build runs after its parent's build, so a parent's set in build is visible.
- `uvm_config_db#(uvm_object)` with a derived config class: set and get must use the same parameter type, then `$cast`.
- Use `+UVM_CONFIG_DB_TRACE` and `check_config_usage()` to find unused or mistyped settings.

### Follow-ups
- *config_db vs resource_db?* `uvm_config_db` is a hierarchy-aware wrapper over `uvm_resource_db`. Resource_db uses plain scope strings.
tongxin-227:
**Key idea:** A `virtual` method is resolved by the **object's actual type at run time**, not by the handle's declared type. Generic code written against a base class, like a scoreboard, driver or printer, then automatically calls each subclass's specialized behavior. New packet types plug in without touching that code.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SB["scoreboard: t.checksum()"] --> H["handle type: base_pkt"]
  H -->|object is eth_pkt| E["eth_pkt::checksum (CRC32)"]
  H -->|object is usb_pkt| U["usb_pkt::checksum (CRC16)"]
  H -->|object is base_pkt| B["base_pkt::checksum (sum)"]
```

### Code
```systemverilog
class base_pkt;
  byte payload[];
  virtual function int checksum();
    int s = 0; foreach (payload[i]) s += payload[i]; return s & 'hFF;
  endfunction
  function string kind(); return "base"; endfunction        // non-virtual
endclass

class eth_pkt extends base_pkt;
  virtual function int checksum();                          // override
    bit [31:0] crc = '1;
    foreach (payload[i]) begin
      crc ^= payload[i];
      repeat (8) crc = crc[0] ? (crc >> 1) ^ 32'hEDB8_8320 : crc >> 1;
    end
    return ~crc;
  endfunction
  function string kind(); return "eth"; endfunction
endclass

class scoreboard;                                           // written once
  function void check(base_pkt t, int dut_crc);
    if (t.checksum() != dut_crc)                            // dynamic dispatch
      $error("%s checksum mismatch", t.kind());             // static: always "base"
  endfunction
endclass
```

| Call through `base_pkt h` pointing at `eth_pkt` | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `h.checksum()` (virtual) | `eth_pkt::checksum` (CRC32) |
| `h.kind()` (non-virtual) | `base_pkt::kind` → "base" |

### Explanation
- UVM is built on this: `do_copy`, `do_compare`, `convert2string`, `body()` of sequences and `run_phase` of components are all virtual and overridden in user classes.
- Combined with the factory, a test can replace a type, and every virtual call through existing base handles reaches the new code.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- The override must have exactly the same prototype (return type, argument types, and directions).
- Forgetting `virtual` in the **base** is the classic bug. Adding it only in the derived class does not help calls made through base handles.
- Constructors (`new`) cannot be virtual. Use the factory for "virtual construction".

### Follow-ups
- *Pure virtual?* `pure virtual function int checksum();` in a `virtual class` forces every concrete subclass to implement it.
tongxin-228:
**Key idea:** Two active input agents drive packets, and ten passive output monitors observe them. The reference model's rule is **conservation plus legal routing**: every accepted input appears on **exactly one** allowed output with an unchanged payload, and nothing appears that was not sent. The dispatch is random, so do not predict *which* output. Check membership in the legal set, and use coverage to show that every input × output pair, contention and back-pressure actually happened.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  subgraph Inputs
    IA0["in_agent0 (active)"]
    IA1["in_agent1 (active)"]
  end
  subgraph DUT_BOX["DUT: random dispatcher"]
    D["2 to 10"]
  end
  subgraph Outputs
    OM["out_monitor 0..9 (passive, + ready driver for back-pressure)"]
  end
  IA0 --> D
  IA1 --> D
  D --> OM
  IA0 -->|ap| SB["scoreboard: pending[uid]"]
  IA1 -->|ap| SB
  OM -->|ap| SB
  IA0 --> COV["coverage: in x out, burst, stall"]
  OM --> COV
  VSEQ["virtual sequence: traffic + ready patterns"] --> IA0
  VSEQ --> IA1
```

### Checks
| Check | How |
| --- | --- |
| no loss | pending map empty at end; per-entry timeout |
| no duplication | an ID removed on first delivery; a second sighting is an error |
| payload integrity | compare the stored copy with the output packet |
| legal destination | `legal_mask(pkt)` from spec (e.g. all 10, or by class) |
| fairness / distribution | count per output; chi-square-like sanity bound over long runs |
| ordering (if spec'd) | per input, sequence numbers increase on each output |
| protocol | SVA on each interface: valid stable until ready, no X |

### Code (scoreboard core)
```systemverilog
function void write_in(pkt p);              // from 2 input monitors
  if (pending.exists(p.uid)) `uvm_error("DUPIN", p.uid)
  pending[p.uid] = p;
endfunction

function void write_out(pkt p);             // from 10 output monitors, p.port set
  if (!pending.exists(p.uid))              `uvm_error("UNEXP", p.uid)
  else begin
    if (!legal_mask(pending[p.uid])[p.port]) `uvm_error("ROUTE", p.uid)
    if (!p.compare(pending[p.uid]))          `uvm_error("DATA",  p.uid)
    per_port_cnt[p.port]++;
    pending.delete(p.uid);                  // a second copy will be UNEXP = duplicate
  end
endfunction
```

### Stimulus plan
- Both inputs together every cycle, single input, idle gaps, long bursts.
- Output back-pressure: all ready, random ready, one output stuck not-ready (the DUT must still dispatch elsewhere if the spec allows), all outputs blocked.
- Reset during traffic; minimum/maximum packet sizes.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Embed a unique ID (input number + counter) in the payload so the outputs can be matched. Without it, identical payloads are ambiguous.
- "Random" in the DUT may be an LFSR. Cover that every output is eventually chosen, and that a blocked output is never chosen if the spec says so.

### Follow-ups
- *Fairness check?* Over N packets, each output's count is within an agreed bound of N/10, or match the LFSR exactly with a white-box model.

**Key idea:** The top module is the static world: it instantiates the **DUT and interfaces**, generates **clock and reset**, publishes **virtual interfaces** through `uvm_config_db`, optionally `bind`s assertions and sets up waveform dumping, then calls **`run_test()`**. From there UVM takes over: it creates the test via the factory and runs the phases build → connect → run → extract/check/report → `$finish`.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant TOP as tb_top
  participant UVM as uvm_root
  participant T as test
  participant E as env/agents
  TOP->>TOP: clk/rst gen, DUT + if instances
  TOP->>UVM: config_db set vif, run_test()
  UVM->>T: factory create (+UVM_TESTNAME)
  UVM->>T: build_phase (top-down)
  T->>E: create env, agents, scoreboard
  UVM->>E: connect_phase (TLM)
  UVM->>E: run_phase (parallel) - sequences drive DUT
  UVM->>E: extract / check / report
  UVM->>TOP: $finish
```

### Code
```systemverilog
`timescale 1ns/1ps
module tb_top;
  import uvm_pkg::*;
  `include "uvm_macros.svh"
  import my_tb_pkg::*;                      // tests, env, agents

  logic clk = 0, rst_n = 0;
  always #5 clk = ~clk;                     // 100 MHz
  initial begin
    rst_n = 0;
    repeat (5) @(posedge clk);
    rst_n <= 1;
  end

  bus_if bif (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n));
  my_dut u_dut (.clk(clk), .rst_n(rst_n), .valid(bif.valid), .ready(bif.ready),
                .data(bif.data));
  bind my_dut my_dut_sva u_sva (.*);        // assertions

  initial begin
    uvm_config_db #(virtual bus_if)::set(null, "uvm_test_top.env.agt*", "vif", bif);
    run_test();                             // test name from +UVM_TESTNAME=...
  end

  initial begin                             // optional waves
    if ($test$plusargs("WAVES")) begin $dumpfile("tb.vcd"); $dumpvars(0, tb_top); end
  end
endmodule
```

| Top module item | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| clock/reset | free-running clock, reset sequence (or driven by a reset agent) |
| interfaces + DUT | pin connection |
| `bind` | attach SVA without editing RTL |
| `config_db::set` | hand vifs to the class world |
| `run_test()` | start UVM; never returns normally |
| timeout, waves | `uvm_top.set_timeout`, dump control |

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- If `rst_n` is generated in the top, the driver must still wait for reset deassertion before driving.
- `run_test("my_test")` hardcodes the default name, and `+UVM_TESTNAME` still wins.
- Put `import uvm_pkg::*` and the testbench package in the top, or the test class is not registered and you get "cannot find test".

### Follow-ups
- *Multiple tests in one compile?* Yes. Every test class is compiled into the package and selected at run time with `+UVM_TESTNAME`.
tongxin-232:
**Key idea:** Verification is "done" when agreed **signoff criteria** are met: every requirement in the reviewed test plan maps to passing tests, checkers or assertions; functional, code and assertion coverage reach their targets, with every hole closed or formally waived; the bug discovery rate has flattened, with no open critical bugs; and regressions are stable across seeds. A coverage number alone is not signoff. It says what was *exercised*, not what was *checked* or what was *missed in the plan*.

| Signoff dimension | Typical evidence | Target example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plan completeness | spec ↔ plan traceability matrix, reviewed with designers/architects | 100% features mapped |
| Functional coverage | covergroups, cover properties | 100% or waived bins |
| Code coverage | line/branch/cond/toggle/FSM | ≥ 95–100% with reviewed exclusions |
| Assertions | non-vacuous pass, formal proofs | all critical properties proven or covered |
| Checking | every output compared (SB/SVA), no disabled checkers | reviewed |
| Bugs | open bug list; trend curve | 0 open P1/P2; find rate ~flat for N weeks |
| Regression | pass rate over many seeds, all configs | ≥ 99–100% for M nights |
| Other | GLS, low-power, CDC/RDC, lint, X-prop reviewed | signed off |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  SPEC["spec"] --> PLAN["test plan + coverage model"]
  PLAN --> TESTS["tests + checkers"]
  TESTS --> REG["regressions"]
  REG --> COV["merged coverage"]
  COV --> HOLES{"holes?"}
  HOLES -->|yes| ACT["new tests / constraints / waiver with reason"]
  ACT --> REG
  HOLES -->|no| BUGS{"bug rate flat, no open critical?"}
  BUGS -->|yes| SIGN["signoff review"]
  BUGS -->|no| REG
```

### Explanation
- **Coverage closure ≠ correctness.** A covergroup can be sampled while the scoreboard is disabled. Review that every coverage point has an associated check.
- The **bug curve** is a confidence indicator: after features freeze, the find rate should drop. A late spike means a weak area.
- Document residual risk: features verified only at system level, waived bins, known limitations.

### Corner cases & pitfalls
- Missing requirements are invisible to coverage. Plan reviews with designers and spec owners catch them.
- Over-constrained random can show 100% on the bins you wrote while never hitting corner interactions. Add crosses and directed corners.
- Excluding code coverage without review hides dead or unreachable bugs.

### Follow-ups
- *How do you prioritize closure when time is short?* Rank by risk: new or changed logic, complex control, past bug density, customer-visible features.
